loText: Calculate the hurdle rate and apply this rate in making business decisions using RAROC.
question:
The CFO of an Australian bank set the firm’s hurdle rate at 8.00% three months ago. The bank’s common equity beta has since been re-estimated, and the next scheduled semi-annual review is three months away. The bank is funded only with common and preferred equity. Current data:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Market value of common equity (AUD billion) | 8.00 |
| Market value of preferred equity (AUD billion) | 4.00 |
| Risk-free rate (%) | 3.50 |
| Expected return on the market portfolio (%) | 8.50 |
| Common equity beta (re-estimated) | 1.40 |
| Yield on preferred shares (%) | 6.00 |

Which of the following best describes the updated hurdle rate and the action the CFO should take?

options.A: 9.00%; keep 8.00% until the semi-annual review, because the hurdle rate is reset only on its scheduled date.
options.B: 10.50%; reset the hurdle rate now, because it has changed by more than 10 percent since it was last set.
options.C: 9.00%; keep 8.00% for now, because the hurdle rate is reset only when the equity market-value weights change.
options.D: 9.00%; reset the hurdle rate now, because it has changed by more than 10 percent since it was last set.

solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank: recompute the hurdle after a beta re-estimate and decide whether to reset early.

The hurdle rate is not fixed forever, because its inputs (equity beta, market returns, risk-free rate, preferred yields and the market values used as weights) move. GARP says “the hurdle rate should be reset periodically, say every six months, or when it has changed by more than 10 percent.” Schweser words the same policy as “perhaps once or twice a year or when it has moved by over 10%”. The two triggers are joined by or: either the calendar review or a material move is enough. question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the capital budgeting process of a Brazilian universal bank, which uses a single after-tax hurdle rate of 10.0% for all businesses. Two units are under review:

- Oil and gas exploration financing: after-tax RAROC of 14.0%, with very volatile returns that move closely with commodity and equity market cycles.
- Retail banking, properly risk-managed: after-tax RAROC of 8.0%, with steady revenues and low volatility.

Management plans to expand the first unit and shrink the second, citing the hurdle rate comparison. Which of the following best describes the consultant’s concern?

options.A: The simple rule does not capture the systematic riskiness of returns, so it may accept the exploration unit even if it lowers firm value and reject the retail unit even if it adds value.
options.B: The simple rule does not capture the systematic riskiness of returns, so it may reject the exploration unit even if it adds value and accept the retail unit even if it lowers firm value.
options.C: The simple rule does not capture expected losses in the numerator, so the exploration unit’s RAROC is overstated relative to the retail unit’s RAROC.
options.D: The simple rule does not use a recent hurdle rate, so resetting the hurdle every six months would rank the exploration unit and the retail unit correctly.

solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank: why comparing a volatile exploration unit and a steady retail unit with one hurdle can mislead.

**Concept and theory**

The simple rule (accept if RAROC is above the hurdle, reject if below) compares every activity with one firm-wide hurdle rate. GARP warns: “applying this simple rule can lead to a firm’s accepting high-risk projects that will lower the value of the firm and rejecting low-risk projects that will increase the value of the firm.” Its examples are oil exploration (very volatile returns) and properly risk-managed retail banking (steady revenues, low volatility).

question: A risk analyst at a German bank is assessing how sensitive a business decision is to a pending re-estimation of the bank’s common equity beta. |---|---|

| Bank’s after-tax hurdle rate (weighted cost of equity) | 9.00 |
| Risk-free rate (three-month Treasury bills) | 1.20 |
| Expected return on the market portfolio | 6.20 |

The beta of the bank’s equity is 1.70. Which of the following best describes the decision under the adjusted RAROC criterion and its basis?

options.A: Accept, because the adjusted RAROC of 1.70% is above the risk-free rate of 1.20%.
options.B: Reject, because the adjusted RAROC of 1.70% is below the hurdle rate of 9.00%.
options.C: Reject, because the adjusted RAROC of 1.70% is below the market excess return of 5.00%.

question:
A junior risk analyst at a US regional bank is asked to compute the adjusted RAROC of a proposed commercial real estate lending project from a data sheet prepared by the planning team. The sheet contains more figures than the calculation needs.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Project RAROC (after tax, %) | 12.00 |
| Bank’s after-tax hurdle rate (%) | 10.50 |
| Risk-free rate, three-month Treasury bills (%) | 3.10 |
| Expected return on the market portfolio, next year (%) | 9.10 |
| Realised return on the market portfolio, last year (%) | 14.00 |
| Beta of the bank’s equity | 1.10 |

The adjusted RAROC that the analyst should report is closest to:
solution:
Stem summary: US regional bank data sheet with excess data: RAROC 12.00%, $r_{f}$ 3.10%, expected $R_{M}$ 9.10%, realised market return 14.00%, $\beta_{E}$ 1.10; compute ARAROC.

**Concept and theory**

loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
question:
A regional commercial bank is considering a 1-year loan to be fully funded by deposits, with the following parameters:

- Loan amount: JPY 4.2 billion
- Average annual interest rate paid on deposits: 0.4%
- Annual interest rate received on loan: 3.2%
- Expected loss: 2.0% of face value of loan
- Annual operating costs: 0.5% of face value of loan
- Economic capital required to support the loan: 10.0%
- Average pre-tax return on economic capital: 1.4%
- Effective tax rate: 38%
- Other transfer costs: JPY 0

What is the after-tax RAROC for this loan?

**Concept**

After-tax RAROC is after-tax risk-adjusted income divided by economic capital:

where ER is expected revenue, ROEC the return on economic capital, IC interest expense, OC operating costs and EL expected loss. The denominator is economic capital, not the loan amount.

All figures in JPY billion. Economic capital = 4.2 × 10% = 0.42.

**Operating costs:** 4.2 × 0.5% = 0.02100

**Expected loss:** 4.2 × 2.0% = 0.08400

loText: Calculate and interpret the RAROC for a project, loan, or loan portfolio and use RAROC to compare business unit performance.
question:
A regional commercial bank is considering a loan with the following parameters that would be fully funded by deposits:

- Loan amount: CNY 3.8 billion
- Average annual interest rate paid on deposits: 0.6%
- Annual interest rate received on loan: 4.1%
- Expected loss: 3.0% of face value of loan
- Annual operating costs: 0.3% of face value of loan
- Economic capital required to support the loan: 15.0%
- Average pre-tax return on economic capital: 2.0%
- Effective tax rate: 38%
- Other transfer costs: CNY 0

What is the after-tax RAROC for this loan?
solution:
**Concept**

Same after-tax RAROC template with new numbers: numerator is expected revenue plus return on economic capital, less interest expense, operating costs and expected loss, all after tax; denominator is economic capital.

**Working**

All figures in CNY million. Economic capital = 3,800 × 15% = 570.

**Pre-tax income:** 155.8 + 11.4 − 22.8 − 11.4 − 114.0 = 19.0

**After tax:** 19.0 × (1 − 0.38) = 11.78

**RAROC:** $\frac{11.78}{570} = 2.07\%$

**Exam trap.** The denominator is economic capital (570), not the loan (3,800). The distractors are: wrong denominator, no tax, and a cost added instead of subtracted.

loText: Calculate the hurdle rate and apply this rate in making business decisions using RAROC.
question:
A risk analyst in the RAROC group at Firm QZK is calculating the hurdle rate to be used in assessing whether some of the firm’s business units are adding value to the firm. The analyst has the following information:

- Firm QZK is funded only with common equity and preferred equity.
- Market value of common equity: GBP 20 billion
- Market value of preferred equity: GBP 8 billion
- Dividend payment on the firm’s preferred equity as a percentage of par value of preferred equity: 6.0%
- Current yield on preferred equity: 4.5%
- Expected return of the market portfolio: 8%
- Volatility of returns of the market portfolio: 20%
- Volatility of returns of Firm QZK’s common equity: 14%
- Correlation between the market return and the return of Firm QZK’s common equity: 0.65

The analyst uses the CAPM to determine the cost of the firm’s common equity and assumes that the risk-free interest rate will remain constant at 3%. What is the correct hurdle rate that the analyst will calculate?
solution:
**Concept**

The hurdle rate is the after-tax weighted average cost of equity capital: $h = \frac{CE \times r_{CE} + PE \times r_{PE}}{CE + PE}$ . The cost of common equity comes from the CAPM with $\beta= \rho\frac{\sigma_{\text{stock}}}{\sigma_{\text{market}}}$ . The cost of preferred equity is its current yield, not its coupon.

**Working**

**Beta:** $0.65 \times\frac{0.14}{0.20} = 0.455$

**Cost of common equity:** 3% + 0.455 × (8% − 3%) = 5.275%

**Hurdle rate:** $\frac{20 \times5.275\% + 8 \times4.5\%}{20 + 8} = \frac{1.055 + 0.360}{28} = 5.05\%$

**Exam trap.** Wrong input twin: dividend rate on par versus current yield. The market’s required return on the preferred shares is the yield. Use market values as weights.

loText: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability.
question: A packaging materials manufacturer is considering a project that has an estimated RAROC of 12%. Suppose that the risk-free rate is 4% per year, the expected market rate of return is 10% per year, and the company’s equity beta is 1.6. The manufacturer uses the adjusted RAROC metric as the criterion to decide whether or not to accept the project. Which of the following correctly describes the decision the company should make and the rationale for making that decision?

options.A: Reject the project because the adjusted RAROC is higher than the market expected excess return.
options.B: Accept the project because the adjusted RAROC is higher than the expected excess return of the market.
options.C: Reject the project because the adjusted RAROC is lower than the risk-free rate.
options.D: Accept the project because the adjusted RAROC is lower than the risk-free rate.

solution:
**Concept**

Adjusted RAROC removes the compensation for systematic risk: ARAROC $= \text{RAROC} - \beta_{E} (R_{M} - R_{F})$. The project adds value only if ARAROC exceeds the risk-free rate.

**Working**

ARAROC = 12% − 1.6 × (10% − 4%) = 12% − 9.6% = 2.4%

2.4% \< 4%, so reject.

**Exam trap.** Two-part options: the decision and the rationale must both be right. The benchmark for ARAROC is the risk-free rate.

loText: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability.
question: An e-commerce entrepreneur is considering a new project with an estimated risk-adjusted return on capital (RAROC) of 12%. His multi-million company has an equity beta of 1.2, and the return on riskfree U.S. Treasury bills stands at 3%. The expected market rate of return is 10% per annum. Using the criterion of adjusted risk-adjusted return on capital (ARAROC), the company should:

options.A: Accept the project because the ARAROC is lower than the market expected excess return
options.B: Reject the project because the ARAROC is lower than the market expected excess return
options.C: Accept the project because the ARAROC is higher than the risk-free rate of return
options.D: Reject the project because the ARAROC is higher than the market expected excess return

solution:
**Concept**

Adjusted RAROC: ARAROC $= \text{RAROC} - \beta_{E} (R_{M} - R_{F})$. The rule is to accept when ARAROC is greater than the risk-free rate.

**Working**

ARAROC = 12% − 1.2 × (10% − 3%) = 12% − 8.4% = 3.6%

3.6% > 3%, so accept.

**Exam trap.** The market excess return is already inside the ARAROC formula. Comparing ARAROC with it again double counts. The benchmark is the risk-free rate.

loText: Calculate the adjusted RAROC for a project to determine its viability.
question: A packaging materials manufacturer is considering a project that has an estimated risk-adjusted return on capital (RAROC) of 15%. Suppose that the risk-free interest rate is 3% per year, the expected market rate of return is 11% per year, and the company’s equity beta is 1.8. Using the criterion of adjusted risk-adjusted return on capital (ARAROC), the company should:

options.A: Accept the project because the ARAROC is higher than the market expected excess return.
options.B: Reject the project because the ARAROC is higher than the market expected excess return.
options.C: Reject the project because the ARAROC is lower than the risk-free interest rate.
options.D: Accept the project because the ARAROC is lower than the risk-free interest rate.

solution:
**Concept**

Same rule with new numbers: ARAROC $= \text{RAROC} - \beta_{E} (R_{M} - R_{F})$, accept only if it exceeds the risk-free rate.

**Working**

ARAROC = 15% − 1.8 × (11% − 3%) = 15% − 14.4% = 0.6%

0.6% \< 3%, so reject.

**Exam trap.** A RAROC of 15% looks attractive on its own. With a beta of 1.8 nearly all of it is compensation for systematic risk. Always finish the calculation before judging.
